Are US Long Bonds A Buy? (Part III)

Will Denyer

Gavekal Research | 7 Sep 2026

Consider a range of forces that have pushed bond yields higher this year. The Federal Reserve has been reducing its holdings of long-term securities, something the Treasury now aims to counter with its upcoming twist operation (see Are US Long Bonds A Buy? (Part I)). Large US budget deficits got even larger as tariff refunds were distributed and the US started a new war in Iran, with only the first of those forces now starting to abate (see Are US Long Bonds A Buy? (Part II)). The Fed is expected to hike policy rates, which has helped keep inflation expectations anchored but may also be pushing up real yields (see A DTR Moment For The Fed And Treasury). Meanwhile, Japanese government bond yields have risen significantly and, while still lower than elsewhere, may now be high enough, combined with an attractively valued currency, to draw capital away from other bond markets (see A Buy Recommendation).Yet the biggest driver may be something else entirely. An extraordinary amount of money is being raised this year to fund artificial intelligence infrastructure. If this is indeed the biggest force pushing yields higher, the key question for bond investors is how long this capital spending and fundraising boom will persist.
